title: Gender and the article
goal: Predict a noun's gender from its ending and pick ο, η or το.

blocks.text: Every Greek noun is masculine, feminine or neuter, and the article in front of it tells you which. Always learn a noun with its article: not *σπίτι* but **το σπίτι**. The good news is that the ending of the nominative singular usually gives the gender away.

blocks.title: Endings that signal gender
head: Gender
Article
Typical endings
Examples
rows: ο δρόμος, ο πατέρας, ο μαθητής, ο καφές
η ώρα, η πόλη, η ζωή
το νερό, το σπίτι, το πρόβλημα

blocks.text: Watch the traps. Some -ος nouns are feminine (η οδός 'street', η μέθοδος 'method'), and words for young people are neuter: **το παιδί** 'child', **το κορίτσι** 'girl', **το αγόρι** 'boy'.

blocks.title: Diminutives turn everything neuter
blocks.text: Greeks use the diminutive **-άκι** constantly, for warmth rather than size, and it is always neuter: **το καφεδάκι** 'a nice little coffee', **το σπιτάκι** 'little house', **ένα νεράκι** 'a drop of water' at the kafeneio. First names do it too: Μαρία becomes **το Μαράκι**, Γιώργος **το Γιωργάκι** (or masculine **ο Γιωργάκης**). Professions often have one form for both sexes, and the article does the work: **ο γιατρός** for a man, **η γιατρός** for a woman, likewise **ο/η δικηγόρος** 'lawyer'.

items.prompt: ___ μέθοδος
items.why: A small group of -ος nouns, many of them learned (μέθοδος, οδός, είσοδος), are feminine.

items.prompt: ___ κορίτσι
items.why: Words for young people (παιδί, κορίτσι, αγόρι) are neuter whatever the sex.

items.prompt: ___ γιατρός (Dr Eleni Pappa)
items.why: Common-gender nouns keep one form; the article shows the person's sex.

___ οδός
items.why: οδός 'street' is a feminine -ος noun, as in street signs: Οδός Ερμού.

items.prompt: ___ αγόρι
items.why: αγόρι 'boy' is neuter like other -ι nouns.
